## Scope and development status

This is the teaching plan for the expanded workshop. The example project,
dataset/model versioning exercises, and privacy demonstration still need to be
developed and tested. The package choices below describe planned roles; they are
not a record of dependencies already restored in the project environment.

The workshop will follow one research project from inputs to archived outputs.
Participants will receive a prepared R project and computing environment so that
most of the practical time can be spent using the workflow. Detailed tool
installation, production model deployment, and a full treatment of differential
privacy are outside the core scope.

## Proposed revised abstract

Open and reproducible science is increasingly important for ensuring that
research can be understood, evaluated, reused, and extended by others. This
workshop provides a practical introduction to developing reproducible research
workflows using R and open-source tools.

Participants will develop an integrated workflow incorporating GitHub, renv,
Docker, targets, Quarto, pins, vetiver, and Zenodo. The workshop will demonstrate
how these tools work together throughout the research lifecycle, from capturing
dependencies and computational environments to organising analyses, producing
reports, and preserving research outputs.

The workshop will introduce research data and model management, including
documenting metadata, tracking provenance, and maintaining versioned datasets
and fitted models with pins and vetiver. Recognising that original research
data cannot always be shared, a focused extension will explore differentially
private synthetic data and the trade-offs between privacy, analytical utility,
and reproducibility. Participants will consider what a shared synthetic dataset
allows others to reproduce and what remains unverifiable without the originals.

Finally, Zenodo will demonstrate the preservation and archiving of permitted
research outputs with persistent identifiers. Throughout the workshop, the
emphasis will be on transparent, portable, auditable, reusable, and accessible
research, with clear documentation of any limits on data access and reuse.

## One practical research project

Use a public, redistributable tabular dataset and a simple fitted model throughout
the exercises. Treat the original data as restricted only for the teaching
scenario; participants will not need confidential data.

1. **Describe and version the inputs.** Record the source, licence, variables,
   units, and processing decisions. Create a local `pins` board with versioning
   enabled, write two dataset versions, and retrieve a specified earlier version.
2. **Run the analysis.** Use `targets` to connect data preparation, model fitting,
   and reporting. Make the selected dataset version an explicit input rather
   than silently reading whichever version is newest.
3. **Record the fitted model.** Demonstrate `vetiver` model storage and retrieval,
   including its input requirements and prediction dependencies. Record the
   training-data version, code revision, model settings, and relevant metrics.
4. **Report the provenance.** Use Quarto to connect the methods and results to
   the dataset and model version identifiers. Keep `renv` and Docker as the
   supporting package and computing environments.
5. **Explore a synthetic-data branch.** Demonstrate a reviewed differential
   privacy method on the public teaching data, compare selected utility measures,
   and rerun the same analysis/reporting workflow on the synthetic output.
   Record which results came from original versus synthetic inputs.
6. **Prepare a permitted release.** Assemble code, documentation, approved data
   and model objects, and a report for sharing through GitHub and archiving with
   Zenodo. Use a prepared example of the archive process rather than requiring
   every participant to publish a live record.

Versioning and metadata do not automatically make a dataset or model appropriate
for public release. A model fitted to restricted originals can itself contain
or reveal sensitive information. Treat original-data models, private evaluation
results, and metadata as separate release decisions; a synthetic dataset does
not confer privacy protection on those other objects.

## Packages and scope

| Package | Planned teaching role | Scope |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [pins](https://pins.rstudio.com/articles/pins.html) | Dataset metadata, explicit version identifiers, hashes, and historical retrieval | Core hands-on exercise |
| [vetiver](https://vetiver.posit.co/get-started/version.html) | Fitted-model versions, input requirements, and prediction dependencies | Short practical demonstration |
| [codebook](https://cran.r-project.org/package=codebook) | Variable descriptions and data dictionaries | Optional metadata extension |
| [DPSynth](https://cran.r-project.org/package=DPSynth) | Candidate for differentially private tabular synthesis | Extension, pending method and implementation review |
| [diffpriv](https://cran.r-project.org/package=diffpriv) | Mechanisms for differentially private statistics and related computations | Optional explanation of underlying principles |

`pins` and `vetiver` support versioned storage, but project-specific provenance
links still need to be supplied as metadata. Enable versioning explicitly for a
local folder board. Use the `renv` lockfile to capture the computational package
environment alongside the model's prediction dependencies.

The privacy package is not yet selected as a tested workshop dependency. Review
its method, privacy assumptions, supported data types, installation requirements,
and behaviour under the project's R version before preparing the exercise. A
package description or a utility/risk score is not an independent verification
of a differential privacy guarantee.

## Teaching formats

### Two-hour format

| Activity | Minutes | Intended result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Principles and prepared-project walkthrough | 15 | Understand the project and environment |
| Reproducible analysis and reporting | 40 | Run the targets pipeline and Quarto report |
| Dataset and model metadata, provenance, and versioning | 25 | Retrieve a dataset version and inspect a linked model version |
| Synthetic data and differential privacy demonstration | 20 | Compare selected utility measures and discuss privacy accounting |
| Sharing, archiving, and discussion | 20 | Identify permitted outputs and inspect an archive example |
| **Total** | **120** | |

### Shorter 90-minute format

| Activity | Minutes |
| --- | --- |
| Principles and prepared-project walkthrough | 15 |
| Reproducible analysis and reporting | 30 |
| Dataset versioning exercise and model demonstration | 25 |
| Privacy and synthetic-data overview | 10 |
| Archiving demonstration and discussion | 10 |
| **Total** | **90** |

For the shorter format, supply completed pipeline/report scaffolding and use
prepared outputs for the privacy overview. Move the fuller synthetic-data
exercise and optional data dictionary to follow-up material. These are reusable
teaching formats; dates, venues, and announced session details belong in
[announcements](../ANNOUNCEMENTS.md).

## Questions for the privacy extension

- Which unit is protected, and what does it mean for two datasets to be neighbours?
- What bounds, preprocessing steps, mechanism, and privacy parameters are used?
- How is privacy loss accounted for when several results or datasets are released?
- Which distributions, relationships, and model results remain useful after synthesis?
- Which analyses can be rerun, and which original-data findings cannot be independently verified?

Ordinary synthesis and adding arbitrary noise are not sufficient to establish
differential privacy. A classroom run on public data can illustrate these
concepts, but its utility comparisons do not establish a privacy guarantee.
Review how randomness and any reproducibility seed are handled before presenting
the exercise as an example of a private release.

Background: [NIST's synthetic-data overview](https://www.nist.gov/blogs/cybersecurity-insights/differentially-private-synthetic-data)
and [guidelines for evaluating differential privacy guarantees](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/226/final).

## Development work

- Select and document the public teaching dataset and simple modelling task.
- Prepare the targets pipeline, Quarto report, and expected outputs.
- Add dataset versioning and explicit model-to-data provenance exercises.
- Select, review, and test the privacy demonstration and its teaching assumptions.
- Test the selected package versions before recording them in `renv.lock` and
  rebuilding the workshop environment.
- Prepare permitted release examples, participant instructions, and a reduced
  path for the shorter teaching format.
